title: Semiconductors and superconductors
summary: Semiconductors from the diode to the chip, and superconductors with zero resistance.
cards.0.p: In a metal, some electrons are free and carry current easily. In an insulator there are no free electrons. In semiconductors such as silicon and germanium, free electrons are few, and their number changes with conditions.
cards.0.svg#0: Energy needed to free an electron
cards.0.svg#7: upper band: free electrons · lower band: bound electrons
cards.0.key: What makes a semiconductor valuable is that its conductivity is in our hands.
cards.0.once.soru: Most phone chips are made of silicon. How does silicon conduct electricity?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.yazi: A little or a lot, depending
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: Silicon is a semiconductor. Its conductivity changes with temperature, light, and doping.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: Silicon has far fewer free electrons than a metal.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: Silicon has a small number of free electrons at room temperature. So it conducts a little.
cards.1.h: Resistance that changes with heat and light
cards.1.p: When a metal heats up, its atoms vibrate a lot and the resistance increases. When a semiconductor heats up or receives light, electrons are freed and the resistance decreases.
cards.1.key: This is how a thermistor senses temperature and a photoresistor senses light. It is also how a street lamp turns on by itself when it gets dark.
cards.2.p: The 4 valence electrons of silicon go into bonds. When a little phosphorus (5 electrons) is added, the fifth electron is left free. This material, in which the extra electrons carry the current, is n-type.
cards.2.key: Even very few dopant atoms increase the conductivity many times over.
cards.3.p: If a little boron is added to silicon, one bond is left one electron short, because boron has 3 electrons. This gap is called a hole. A hole moves opposite to the electrons and behaves like a positive charge. This material is called p-type.
cards.3.key: A doped crystal is still neutral. The letters n and p tell the sign of the charge that carries the current.
cards.4.p: When p-type and n-type are joined, a depletion region forms at the boundary. When the plus is connected to p, current flows (forward bias). When it is reversed, it does not. This is a diode.
cards.4.key: A silicon diode starts to conduct at about 0.7 V. This is how chargers turn alternating current into direct current.
cards.4.etk.soru: Does the lamp light up? Put each connection in the right group (silicon diode, lamp in series).
cards.4.etk.ogeler.2.2: In reverse the barrier thickens, and no current flows.
cards.4.etk.ogeler.3.2: The voltage is large, but the direction is reversed. The diode does not conduct.
cards.4.etk.ogeler.4.2: Forward, but less than 0.7 V: the barrier cannot be overcome.
cards.5.h: LED: a diode that gives light
cards.5.p: In a forward-biased LED, electrons combine with holes and give off the energy as light. As the energy gap grows, the light shifts from red to blue.
cards.5.svg#0: A larger energy gap gives light of higher energy
cards.5.key: The blue LED won a Nobel Prize in 2014. An LED gives the light of an incandescent bulb with about one fifth of the energy.
cards.6.p: A solar cell is a wide p-n junction. Light creates electron-hole pairs. The electric field of the junction separates them, and a direct current flows in the circuit.
cards.6.key: The efficiency of silicon panels is about 20-23%. The rest of the light turns into heat or is reflected.
cards.7.p: A transistor controls a large current with a small signal. It can amplify the current or switch it on and off like a switch. In a classic transistor the signal is the base current. In the transistors in chips (MOSFETs), the signal is the gate voltage.
cards.7.key: The 0 and 1 in a computer are these on and off states. The tens of billions of transistors in a phone processor are MOSFETs driven by a gate voltage.
cards.8.p: Processors, memory, camera sensors, LED displays, and solar panels are semiconductors. That is why chip manufacturing is strategic.
cards.8.key: The chip shortage of 2021 stopped many car factories for weeks.
cards.8.once.soru: What is the very pure silicon in chips obtained from?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: The silicon dioxide in sand is refined and turned into extremely pure silicon.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: Steel is made from iron ore, not silicon.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: Fuel and plastics are obtained from petroleum.
cards.9.p: In 1911, when mercury was cooled below 4.2 K, its resistance suddenly became zero. This is called superconductivity. This limiting temperature is called the critical temperature.
cards.9.svg#1: mercury: resistance exactly zero at 4.2 K
cards.9.key: The resistance is exactly zero, but within certain limits. If the temperature exceeds the critical temperature, the magnetic field the critical field, or the current the critical current, superconductivity breaks down.
cards.10.p: A superconductor pushes the magnetic field out of its interior. This is called the Meissner effect. That is why a magnet lowered over it stays suspended in the air.
cards.10.key: A magnet floating in the air is the best-known demonstration of superconductivity.
cards.10.once.soru: What do you look for to prove that a material is a superconductor?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: Both properties are needed together. Low resistance alone can also appear for other reasons.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: A measurement error can also show a resistance near zero. That is why field expulsion is looked for too.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: Not every material that is cooled becomes a superconductor.
cards.11.p: The ceramic YBCO, found in 1987, is a superconductor below 92 K. That is enough for cooling with cheap liquid nitrogen (77 K).
cards.11.svg#8: above 77 K, liquid nitrogen is enough
cards.11.key: There is still no superconductor that works at room temperature. The biggest obstacle is the cost of cooling.
cards.12.p: The powerful magnets of MRI machines are superconducting coils. A superconducting maglev train reached 603 km/h in 2015.
cards.12.svg#6: zero resistance: large current, no heating
cards.12.svg#7: Cooling is costly, but the gain is large
cards.12.key: Zero resistance means a very large current and a very strong field without heating, up to the critical current. CERN's magnets and many quantum computers are superconducting too.
cards.12.once.soru: Why are the coils of a hospital MRI machine cooled with liquid helium?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: The resistance of the cold coil is zero. The coil carries a very large current without heating and produces a strong field.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.yazi: To keep the magnet from melting
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: The coil does not heat anywhere near melting. The aim of the cooling is to bring the resistance to zero.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: A strong magnetic field gives the image. That field is produced by the superconducting coil.
cards.13.p:
• The conductivity of a semiconductor changes with temperature, light, and doping.
• Electrons carry the current in n-type, and holes in p-type.
• A diode passes current in one direction.
• An LED gives light, and a solar cell produces current.
• A transistor controls a large current.
• The resistance of a superconductor is zero.
quiz.0.q: Put each application in a group by the material it relies on.
quiz.0.e: LEDs, solar panels, processors, and thermistors work with a p-n junction or a doped semiconductor. MRI, maglev, and accelerator magnets produce very strong fields with zero-resistance superconducting coils.
quiz.1.q: Match the concepts with their jobs.
quiz.1.ciftler.3.1: Controls a large current with a small signal
quiz.1.e: Phosphorus doping brings extra electrons, and boron doping brings holes. Joining p and n makes a diode. In a transistor, a small signal (base current or gate voltage) switches a large current on and off.
quiz.2.q: Put the events in a solar cell in order (the first one at the top).
quiz.2.ogeler.0: A photon is absorbed at the junction
quiz.2.ogeler.2: The junction field pushes the electron to n and the hole to p
quiz.2.ogeler.3: Current flows in the external circuit
quiz.2.e: Light first frees an electron, and a hole is left behind. The electric field of the junction separates the two. The separated charges travel around the external circuit and make a current.
quiz.3.q: The resistance of a material increases when it is cooled and decreases when it is heated. Which is this material most likely to be?
quiz.3.e: When a semiconductor heats up, more electrons are freed and its resistance decreases. In metals the opposite happens.
quiz.3.y.0: When a metal heats up, its atoms vibrate more and the resistance increases.
quiz.3.y.2: Below the critical temperature, the resistance of YBCO is exactly zero and does not change.
quiz.3.y.3: Silver is also a metal, and its resistance increases when it heats up.
A:ozet: Change resistance by heating, and move charges in doped silicon. Reverse a diode, pick an LED color, and draw current from a solar cell and a transistor. Cool a superconductor and float a magnet in the air.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Lower the temperature and watch the two curves.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: Which one's resistance increases as it cools?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: In cooling silicon the free electrons become fewer, and no charge is left to carry the current. So the resistance increases.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: As copper cools, its atoms vibrate less and its resistance decreases.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Look at the curves: one goes down and the other goes up. A metal and a semiconductor behave in opposite ways.
A:adimlar.1.baslik: Where does the extra electron go?
A:adimlar.1.metin: Phosphorus has been added to silicon. The 5th electron of phosphorus does not go into a bond and is left free. A battery has been connected, making the left end − and the right end +.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: When the battery is connected, which way does the extra electron go?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: An electron is negatively charged and is attracted to the positive end. The extra electron, free to move in the crystal, carries the current.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Charges of the same sign repel each other. So the electron moves away from the − end.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Since the fifth electron is not in a bond, it is freed easily and moves in the electric field.
A:adimlar.2.metin: Now boron has been added instead of phosphorus. Boron comes with 3 electrons, and one bond is left one electron short. This gap is called a hole.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: With the battery connected, which way does the hole go?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Neighboring electrons hop into the hole on their way toward the + end. With each hop the hole shifts one step the opposite way, toward the − end. A hole behaves like a positive charge.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The electrons go toward the + end. The hole moves opposite to them.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: A hole does not stay put. When a neighboring electron hops into it, the hole moves to that electron's old place.
A:adimlar.3.metin: We joined p-type and n-type and got a diode. The plus end of the battery is on the n side, and the voltage is 2.5 V.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: In reverse, the depletion region at the junction thickens and no current flows. If you turn the battery around, the lamp lights up.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: In reverse the current is almost zero. So the lamp does not light at all.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The voltage is high, but the direction is wrong. A diode passes current only from p to n.
A:adimlar.4.metin: In an LED, as the energy gap grows, the color of the light shifts from red to blue. Change the gap and find the material that gives blue light.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: The wavelength of blue light is about 450-490 nm, and the energy gap is about 2.5-2.8 eV. It was hard to make a high-quality gallium nitride crystal with such a large gap. That is why the blue LED came last.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.ipucu: The energy gap grows as you go from red to blue.
A:adimlar.5.metin: Adjust the irradiance on the panel, that is the light power per square meter (W/m²). Get 150 W of power from a 1 m² panel. The efficiency of the panel is 20%.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: 0.20 × 750 W/m² × 1 m² = 150 W. At noon on a clear summer day, solar irradiance is about 1000 W/m². This panel gives about 200 W at most.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.ipucu: Power is found with 0.20 × irradiance × 1 m². What is 150 ÷ 0.20?
A:adimlar.6.metin: In this classic (BJT) transistor, adjust the base current so that 3 mA flows through the collector. The current is amplified 100 times.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.tamam: 30 µA × 100 = 3000 µA = 3 mA. A small base current controls a current 100 times larger. This is called an amplifier.
A:adimlar.7.metin: A ceramic disk (YBCO) will be cooled with liquid nitrogen. Then a magnet will be lowered over the disk.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.soru: What happens when the magnet comes near the disk?
A:adimlar.7.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The cooled disk becomes a superconductor and pushes the magnet's field out of its interior. This is called the Meissner effect. The magnet hovers above the disk.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: A ceramic is not attracted like iron. In the superconducting state it does the opposite and pushes the field out.
A:adimlar.7.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: That would happen at room temperature. The cold disk is a superconductor and pushes the field out.
A:adimlar.8.metin: Change the temperature and find the highest temperature at which YBCO stays superconducting.
A:adimlar.8.gorev.tamam: YBCO is a superconductor below about 92 K. Liquid nitrogen (77 K) is enough for this, and expensive liquid helium is not needed.
A:adimlar.8.gorev.ipucu: Go just below the point where the green curve drops to zero.
A:kapanis.0: The type of dopant decides which charge carries the current. Electrons carry it in n-type, and holes in p-type.
A:kapanis.1: A diode passes current only in the forward direction. The color of an LED is set by its energy gap.
A:kapanis.2: A transistor controls a large current with a small signal (base current or gate voltage).
A:kapanis.3: Below the critical temperature, critical field, and critical current, a superconductor drops to zero resistance and pushes the magnetic field out.
